speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Hey everybody, Peter Zion here coming to you from a snowy Colorado where we're in the column

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: between the storms. Two feet behind us, one foot in front of us, lots of shoveling yet to be done.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Today we're taking an entry from the Patreon forum. The question specifically is can China

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: use immigration to solve some of its problems? The scale of the challenge of course is huge and

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: what China has done isn't really technically immigration. They send their people out to

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: attend universities and pick up technical skills that they can't get within China and then they try

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: to bring them back. And that has been at least moderately successful. I'd say probably a third

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: to half of the students they send abroad come back and considering that's better than zero. You know,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: take the win where you can get it. But moving the demographic pendulum is really hard and takes

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: decades, even with immigration. So let me give you a quick three examples. Canada decided about 15,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: 17 years ago that they were facing a European style demographic collapse. And so they opened up the

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: doors and over the course of the next 15 to 17 years brought in about 4 million people, mostly under

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: age 40. That did stabilize their tax base, that did stabilize their workforce, but it generated 4 million

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: people who needed a place to live. And if you need a place to live, you're not very price sensitive.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: So it caused a housing shortage across the system in the places where actually there was work.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: And they're now dealing with the political outcomes of that, which is part of the reason why the

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Justin Trudeau government is likely to fall on elections next year. Second example would be

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Germany, where the birth rate has been dropping for 130 years, ever since industrialization began.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: But it really fell off the cliff after reunification in 1990. Now you would think that you have a big

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: optimistic moment like reunification and birth rate would go up. The problem is that the East German

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: territories, former East Germany, were economic basket cases. And the Germans collectively spent over a

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: trillion euro trying to rehabilitate the industrial plant and infrastructure, and it was just a waste of

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: money. So if you're in the East German system, you saw all this money coming in to try to make your

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: system better, and it all failed. And in the meantime, all your young people left, and so your birth rate

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: almost went to zero. And in the West German system, you're paying, and you're paying, and you're paying,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: and you're paying, and you're paying. And you basically had a 12-year period with negligible

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: economic growth because you were basically shoveling money into the furnace. So the birth rate dropped

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: there too. And of course, it's a heavily industrialized, urbanized country. And when you live in condos,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: there's no room for the kids, as opposed to when you live on the farm. There's all kinds of room for

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: them, not to mention their free labor. So the economic case went away. The emotional case went away,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: and the birth rate in Germany kept falling. And probably within the next seven or eight years,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: we're looking at about a one-third reduction in the size of the German workforce, and it will only

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: shrink thereafter with all the implications it has for consumption, tax base, and state coherence.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: So a few years ago, the Germans let in about a million people from Syria refugees. And people are

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: like, oh, this is for demographics. No, they just did that because they were trying to do the morally

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: correct thing. Because of the million people, something like 850,000 of them were men. And

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: that really doesn't help the demographic situation in the long run. And that's before you consider

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: things like language and cultural and skills barriers. If the Germans really wanted to solve

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: their demographic problem with immigration, they would need to bring in about 2 million people a year

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: under age 25 every year from now on just to hold the line. You know, after 20 years, it's not Germany

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: anymore. If you're going to use immigration to stave off a demographic problem, you need to do two

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: things. One, you need to start early before you have much of a problem. And two, you have to have

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: some assimilative capacity so you don't generate big culture clashes. You want it to be a trickle,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: not a flood. Which brings us to China. Chinese data is getting updated bit by bit by bit by bit by

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: bit. They're trying to get a grip on their demographic problem. And with a population of

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: what they thought was 1.3 billion, now looks like it's closer to 1.1 billion, may even be less than 1

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: billion. The scale of what they would need to do is immense. Now, also, the trajectory of the

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Chinese is far worse than the Germans. The Germans industrialized over 130 years. The Chinese did it in

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: about 45. So if you just go back to like 1960, the Chinese birth rate was so high that each woman was

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: having four to six kids. And Mao was concerned that the young generation was going to eat the country

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: alive, perhaps literally. So they instituted a two-child policy, which shortly thereafter became a one-child

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: policy. And then the country went through the fastest industrialization process ever. So everyone moved off

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: of the farm and into condos and stopped having kids. We're now in a situation where officially the

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: birth rate is about 1.2 children per woman. The reality is probably below one. And we already know

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: by official data that in most of the major cities, places like Shanghai or Beijing, it's already below 0.4

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: 0.5. So you're talking about one-fourth, one-fifth replacement levels. That means that we're looking

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: at a complete demographic collapse of the Chinese system within 10 years. I mean, the Germans are

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: practically a slow fade out compared to what's happening in China. And the challenge, numerically,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: if you wanted to use immigration, is you're probably talking about needing to get 30 million people

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: under age 25 every year just to sustain the numbers where they are today. I'm not sure there are that

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: many potential migrants in the world at any given time. So we're looking at a workforce collapse. We're

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: looking at a financial collapse. We're looking at a state coherence collapse in the not-too-distant

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: future. The real challenge isn't how do you save China. It's gone. We're just basically marking

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: time. The challenge in the short term is preparing for its fall because when that industrial plant goes

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: away, we're going to feel it. The second challenge a few years from now is how do you manage a post-China

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: Asia where China is in degradation, de-civilization, and chaos. And then the longer term challenge for the

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: latter half of this century will be what do you do when what was the world's largest ethnic group

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: vanishes from this world. Because when you break down the industrial base, and we're already in a

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: country where there's more people over age 50 than under age 50, and they age out to the point that

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: they can't even maintain their infrastructure. We have a sort of international crisis that we have

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: never seen before. The Chinese are leading the way, and hopefully in their fall and dissolution,

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: we can find some lessons that will help us manage other parts of the world that are experiencing

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: extreme demographic decline because they're not alone.
